chunk_findings.detail: The TOML branch decides registration by a raw substring search of the whole file: `return "ddflow" in path.read_text(...)`, whereas the JSON branch checks the actual server names via `get_servers(data, h.mcp.shape)`. Any occurrence of the substring anywhere in the file satisfies it. Given an agent whose MCP file (`h.mcp.shape == SHAPE_TOML`) contains a comment such as `# ddflow hooks are installed separately`, or a table for an unrelated server like `[mcp_servers.ddflow_backup]`, while no `ddflow` MCP server is actually registered, `mcp_registered` returns `True`, `_findings` (line 159) emits no `mcp` finding, and `harness_doctor` reports "nothing is broken" for an agent whose MCP server is in fact not registered — exactly the drift `doctor` is supposed to surface. The substring must be checked against parsed server keys, in the same way the JSON branch does.

chunk_findings.detail: An existing-but-unparseable MCP file is reported as if nothing were registered. `read_json` returns an `Unreadable` instance on a read/parse failure, and line 120 collapses that to `False` via `not isinstance(data, Unreadable) and ...`; `_findings` then emits `f"no ddflow server in {h.mcp.path}"` with remedy `ddflow adopt --agents {h.id}`. So for a malformed or unreadable JSON config the operator is told there is no server and pointed at an install/adopt command, when the correct statement is that the file cannot be read. This is also inconsistent with the sibling `_hook_findings`, which has an explicit `if on is None: ... f"{spec.file} cannot be read: {why}"` branch, and with the module docstring's rule that an unknown fact is not an absence. `mcp_registered` needs a third state (unknown) that `_findings` renders as a read failure with no destructive remedy.

chunk_findings.detail: `mcp_registered` decides a TOML-shaped MCP file is fine by raw substring search over the whole file text: `return "ddflow" in path.read_text(...)`. That does not answer the question in its own docstring ("Is a `ddflow` server in the agent's project MCP file?"). Any occurrence of the string elsewhere makes it report `True`. Concrete case: a repo whose TOML MCP config was human-edited, with the server entry removed but a header comment such as `# ddflow owns this file` (or any retained line mentioning a `ddflow` tool/path, e.g. `[mcp_servers.ddflow-old]`), still contains `ddflow`, so `mcp_registered` returns `True`, `_findings` (line 160) adds no MCP finding, and `harness_doctor` prints "nothing is broken" with exit OK even though `ddflow adopt --agents <id>` is exactly what is needed. Note the JSON branch one line below is exact (`"ddflow" in get_servers(...)` tests keys), so the two shapes disagree about what counts as registered — the TOML branch should parse the document or at least match a table/key, not the file's bytes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/harness.py:119

chunk_findings.detail: For every `harness_*` action the payload is the single tuple `("harnesses", "id", "levels", "features", "findings")`, but the three subcommands that the same conditional dispatches to produce disjoint fact sets: `harness_list` returns the `harnesses` list, `harness_show` returns `id`/`levels`/`features`, and `harness_doctor` returns `findings`. The `payload` is documented as "the FACTS" from which the JSON body is built (and `message` is deliberately absent from it so it "stays OUT of the JSON body"), i.e. the body builder resolves each declared key against `data`. Given `ddflow_hooks(action="harness_list")` the body builder is therefore handed `id`, `levels`, `features` and `findings`, none of which the list result carries (the same for `harness_doctor` with `id`/`levels`/`features`/`harnesses`), so the call raises `KeyError` — or, if the builder happens to tolerate absent keys, it emits null fact fields that were never computed, contradicting the intended per-subcommand output ("list: agents and whether adopted here; show <id>: … levels … and features; doctor: drift, dangling commands, missing hooks"). The sibling CLI handler `cmd_harness` (ddflow/surfaces/commands/harness.py:14) avoids exactly this by passing only `tuple(k for k in out.data if k != "message")`; the declared payload needs the same per-action scoping instead of one union tuple.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/hooks.py:246 (the new `payload=lambda a: ...`, harness branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-change resolution chain in `sessions.py` was `("DDFLOW_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID")`. After this change the chain is built from `HR.session_env_vars()`, which is seeded with `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV[0]` (`DDFLOW_SESSION_ID`), then the descriptors' `[env] session_id` entries, then `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` — and `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` is `("DDFLOW_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_SESSION_ID")`. `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` has been dropped from the fallback list entirely, yet the comment directly above it claims these are "Environment variables an older ddflow or another tool already set for a session id; kept after the descriptors' so nothing that worked stops working". Concrete input: a Claude Code process that exports `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (and not `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID`), on an install where the descriptors' `[env] session_id` lists do not include it (or where `load()` yields nothing, e.g. a broken/absent descriptor directory). Before the change, line 198 turned that variable into the harness session id and the session was attributed (`return hid, "harness"`); now the loop never looks at it, the session id is not found in `live`, and the session silently falls through to the `"implicit"` branch with `HR.detect` also unable to name the harness. Either the descriptor for Claude is assumed to re-declare the variable — in which case the CLAUDE_SESSION_ID retained in `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` is dead weight and the asymmetry is unexplained — or this is a compat regression that contradicts the stated intent of the very constant that was added.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessreg.py:349 (LEGACY_SESSION_ENV / session_env_vars)

chunk_findings.detail: The change states that "today only CLAUDE_SESSION_ID / CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID are read", and `test_every_descriptor_variable_is_consulted_in_resolution_order` confirms both Claude variables are known session variables (`"CLAUDE_SESSION_ID" in vars_` plus the "every descriptor variable is consulted" loop). Yet no test asserts what `detect()` returns for a Claude variable at all — the only detection cases exercised are GEMINI and QWEN_CODE — and the only ambiguity case is two variables belonging to *different* harnesses. A Claude Code process that exports both `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (i.e. two known variables, one harness) hits the exact shape that `detect()` is asserted to answer with `""` for two variables at once. Consequence, per `test_an_implicit_session_records_the_detected_tool`: instead of resuming the real Claude session, `S.resolve` falls through to the "implicit" branch and starts a fresh session, so the harness name is never recorded and the session is split — the opposite of the stated goal ("so per-agent metrics and brief text can name it"). The test file as written would stay green through that regression.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_harness_identity_env.py::test_detect_names_the_harness_whose_variable_is_set / test_two_harnesses_at_once_are_not_guessed_between

chunk_findings.detail: This test seeds an existing session with `log.append("session.started", sid, {"model": "", "tool": ""})` and then asserts only the returned tuple `== (sid, "harness")`. It never asserts that the resumed session's event acquires the detected harness name. The promise of the change is "record which harness a session came from"; the implicit path is checked for this (`started[0].data["tool"] == "qwen"`) but the harness path is not. So an implementation of `resolve` that returns `how="harness"` while leaving `data["tool"]` as `""` for that `session.started` event passes the suite, and per-agent metrics/brief text for every resumed (non-implicit) session remain unnamed. The straightforward additional assertion — `started[0].data["tool"] == "gemini"` on the sid appended in this test — is missing.

chunk_findings.detail: The dispatcher routes to this helper whenever *any* of `--claude`, `--gemini` or `--harness <id>` is set, so a combined invocation is accepted, but the helper only forwards `harness` to the style-writer path when *both* `claude` and `gemini` are false; otherwise `harness` is dropped on the floor and `_agent_hooks(repo, action, claude=claude, gemini=gemini)` runs instead. Input: `ddflow hooks install --claude --harness copilot`. Result: the Claude entry is written, `_harness_hooks`/`HW.apply` is never called for copilot, no `--harness` writer runs, and the returned outcome is `O.ok(...)` with no mention of the skipped harness — the user is told the operation succeeded while one of the explicitly requested configurations was silently not applied. A user asking for two styles in one command (exactly what "writers by style, not by agent" invites) gets a success exit code and half the job.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:_agent_hooks_outcome (the `if not (claude or gemini)` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring states "a style with no writer is refused", and the parallel "this ddflow cannot do what you asked, nothing is broken" case in `_agent_hooks_outcome` (`CH.NewerSettings`) is deliberately mapped to `O.refused("hooks", ..., message=..., installed=...)` with the comment "upgrade, not a failure". This branch instead returns `O.failed("hooks", why, message=why, installed=E.installed(repo))`. Input: `ddflow hooks install --harness <id whose descriptor style has no writer>`. The command installs nothing but reports a *failure* rather than a refusal, so scripts/automation that distinguish the two (and that keep going on a refusal, cf. the NewerSettings path) treat an unimplemented-but-harmless style as a hard error, contradicting the contract the function itself documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:_harness_hooks (`except HW.Unsupported`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The writer is documented (and the change's intent states) as chosen by the descriptor's `style`/`file`/`events`, "not by agent name", and `unsupported()` exists precisely to refuse a harness whose descriptor cannot be written. But `specs()` short-circuits on the built-in table before ever consulting the descriptor:

    if table := tuple(s for s in CH.HOOKS if s.agent == h.id):
        return table

Any harness whose id is `claude` (or `gemini`) therefore keeps writing the table's file/events even when its descriptor says otherwise. Concretely, a descriptor with `[hooks] style = "none"` (the operator disabling hooks for that harness), `hooks` absent/None, or `file = ".claude/settings.local.json"` will still cause `apply()` to install the table rows into `.claude/settings.json`: `specs()` returns the table, `rows` is non-empty, and `apply()`'s `raise Unsupported(...)` is never reached, so the `"none" has nothing to install` / "not VERIFIED" / file checks are bypassed. Either the descriptor is authoritative (then the table branch must be gated by `unsupported(h)` and must not override `hk.file`/`hk.events`), or the module cannot claim descriptor-driven selection.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/hookwriters/__init__.py:38 (specs)

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard that is supposed to reject non-project files only rejects a bare `~` prefix and non-`.json` names:

    if not hk.file.endswith(".json") or hk.file.startswith("~"):
        return f"{h.id}: its hook file {hk.file} is not a project JSON file ddflow writes"

The message claims project-only enforcement, but an expanded user-scope path such as `[REDACTED:path]`, a Windows path `C:\Users\u\...\hooks.json`, `${HOME}/...`, or any `../`-escaping relative path ends with `.json` and does not start with `~`, so `unsupported()` returns `""` and `apply()` installs/uninstalls in that location (this matters directly for the VS Code/harness user-scope path called out in the session context). The same spelling inconsistency means `[REDACTED:path]` is refused while the equivalent absolute path is accepted, so install and status disagree about whether the harness is supported.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/hookwriters/__init__.py:32 (unsupported)

chunk_findings.detail: `fix_for` is keyed by settings-file path and built with a dict comprehension, so it is last-wins: when more than one hook spec in `rows` has the same `s.file`, only the flag of the last spec survives. `check_settings` then emits that single command as the remedy for *any* dangling ddflow command found in that file. The generalisation in this change makes shared files realistic: the session-context states that the Local/VS Code harness reads `.claude/settings.json` hooks and that VS Code's hooks live under `.github/hooks/*.json`, so a descriptor for that harness can declare the same file (or `.github/hooks` dir) as the claude-json (or copilot) descriptor. Concretely, if `rows` contains `spec(file=".claude/settings.json", flag="--claude")` followed by `spec(file=".claude/settings.json", flag="--harness vscode")`, a dangling command that came from the claude-json install is reported with the fix `ddflow hooks install --harness vscode`; running it reinstalls the wrong style and leaves the flagged command in place (the reverse ordering silently prefers `--claude` for the vscode-owned entry). The pre-change code could not hit this because the fix was computed per-path from a single `HOOKS` table with an explicit `gemini` branch. Keying the fix by marker (or collecting all flags for a shared file) would preserve the correct remedy.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/launchers.py:120 (`fix_for` in `check_settings`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that installing the "cursor" harness is refused with `no hook writer for harness 'cursor'` (exit 1, no `.cursor` created), but the stated intent of this change lists "cursor hooks" as one of the writer styles that the descriptor chooses between: "Hook config writers by style, not by agent: claude-json, copilot hooks dir, codex hooks.json, cursor hooks, opencode plugin, none." If the cursor-harness descriptor's style is the "cursor hooks" style (the only reading under which that listed style is used by any harness), then `ddflow hooks install --harness cursor` in a repo exits 0 and writes the cursor hook file, so `assert code == 1` fails. If instead the implementation really has no cursor writer, then the cursor style listed in the intent is not implemented at all. Either way the change is internally inconsistent: the test can only pass if the "cursor hooks" style promised by the intent does not exist, and it fails as soon as that writer is present. Concretely: a repo where `HR.get("cursor").hooks.style == "cursor"` makes line 66's command succeed, breaking line 67's `assert code == 1` and the "no hook writer" message check on line 68.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_hook_writers.py:66 (test_a_style_without_a_writer_is_refused_not_ignored)

chunk_findings.detail: The new function documents its contract as "a style with no writer is refused" (and the change intent repeats "a style with no writer is refused"), but the `HW.Unsupported` branch returns `O.failed("hooks", why, message=why, installed=E.installed(repo))`, while the very next branches in the same helper return `O.refused(...)` for `CH.NewerSettings`. Scenario: `ddflow hooks install --harness <id>` where the descriptor names an agent whose hook style has no writer yet (the intent lists styles such as `none`); the user gets a hard failure outcome instead of the refusal outcome the helper promises, so any caller/renderer that distinguishes refused from failed (as the `NewerSettings` "upgrade, not a failure" path does) reports the wrong kind. Either the branch should return `O.refused(...)` or the docstring/intent claim is wrong; as written the code and its stated contract disagree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:867 (`_harness_hooks`, `HW.Unsupported` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `unsupported()` is the only barrier between a descriptor's `[hooks].file` and a write, and it only rejects two shapes: a missing `.json` suffix and a literal leading `~`. Its own error message claims the rule is "not a **project** JSON file ddflow writes", but the test does not enforce containment in the repo at all. Concretely: a descriptor with `style = "claude"`, `file = "[REDACTED:path]"` (or `"../outside.json"`, or a Windows `C:\...json`) passes `not hk.file.endswith(".json") or hk.file.startswith("~")` as false, so `unsupported()` returns `""`, `specs()` generates rows, and `apply()` calls `CH.install_spec(repo, s)`. `pathlib`'s join discards `repo` for an absolute operand, so the hook is written to the user's real global config during a repo-scoped `install` (and silently removed by `uninstall`), i.e. the class of user-scope write the guard was added to prevent. This is not hypothetical for the case the session-context singles out: VS Code user scope is an absolute path, which on many platforms does not begin with `~`, so the explicit `~` check catches only one spelling of the very thing it is meant to refuse. The check should reject any path that is not repo-relative (e.g. via `Path(hk.file).is_absolute()` plus `PurePosixPath(hk.file).parts[0] != ".."`), not just the tilde spelling.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/hookwriters/__init__.py:43

chunk_findings.detail: The new argument `harness=harness if harness not in ("claude", "gemini") else ""` drops the requested harness name for both `claude` *and* `gemini`, but only `claude` is compensated for: the very next line sets `claude=True` when `harness == "claude"`, whereas nothing anywhere in this call carries the gemini request. `harness` came from `getattr(a, "harness", "")`, and the only other selector passed to `A.hooks` is the `claude` boolean. So for the input `ddflow hooks install --harness gemini` the call becomes `A.hooks(..., harness="", claude=False, ...)`, i.e. indistinguishable from a bare `ddflow hooks install` with no harness at all. Now that writers are selected by descriptor/style (the point of this change), the gemini writer is never selected by name; the request silently falls through to the default writer (or to nothing), and because the previous `if harness and harness not in ("claude", "gemini"): ... return FAIL` guard was removed, the user gets no error indicating gemini was ignored. The `("claude", "gemini")` tuple looks copied verbatim from the guard that was deleted; the pass-through should exclude only `claude` (or gemini needs its own flag/argument).

chunk_findings.detail:
The change's own intent states the writers are selected "by style" and enumerates the styles it implements as "claude-json, copilot hooks dir, codex hooks.json, **cursor hooks**, opencode plugin, none" — i.e. `cursor` is one of the styles this change is supposed to ship a writer for. This test instead hard-codes `cursor` as the canonical example of a harness that has *no* writer:

```python
code, out, err = run_cli(repo, "hooks", "install", "--harness", "cursor")
assert code == 1
assert "no hook writer for harness 'cursor'" in out + err and not (repo / ".cursor").exists()
```

Given the stated intent, either the implementation registers a `cursor hooks` writer (in which case this test fails: `code` will be `0`, output will not contain "no hook writer", and `.cursor/…` will be created) or it does not (in which case the change does not deliver the "cursor hooks" style it claims). One of the two is necessarily wrong; the test encodes the opposite of the delivered feature, so it is either a guaranteed red test or evidence the cursor writer is missing. No input other than simply running the suite is needed to expose this.

chunk_findings.detail: The TOML branch decides registration by a raw substring search of the whole file: `return "ddflow" in path.read_text(...)`, whereas the JSON branch checks the actual server names via `get_servers(data, h.mcp.shape)`. Any occurrence of the substring anywhere in the file satisfies it. Given an agent whose MCP file (`h.mcp.shape == SHAPE_TOML`) contains a comment such as `# ddflow hooks are installed separately`, or a table for an unrelated server like `[mcp_servers.ddflow_backup]`, while no `ddflow` MCP server is actually registered, `mcp_registered` returns `True`, `_findings` (line 159) emits no `mcp` finding, and `harness_doctor` reports "nothing is broken" for an agent whose MCP server is in fact not registered — exactly the drift `doctor` is supposed to surface. The substring must be checked against parsed server keys, in the same way the JSON branch does.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/harness.py:118 (`mcp_registered`, TOML branch)

chunk_findings.detail: An existing-but-unparseable MCP file is reported as if nothing were registered. `read_json` returns an `Unreadable` instance on a read/parse failure, and line 120 collapses that to `False` via `not isinstance(data, Unreadable) and ...`; `_findings` then emits `f"no ddflow server in {h.mcp.path}"` with remedy `ddflow adopt --agents {h.id}`. So for a malformed or unreadable JSON config the operator is told there is no server and pointed at an install/adopt command, when the correct statement is that the file cannot be read. This is also inconsistent with the sibling `_hook_findings`, which has an explicit `if on is None: ... f"{spec.file} cannot be read: {why}"` branch, and with the module docstring's rule that an unknown fact is not an absence. `mcp_registered` needs a third state (unknown) that `_findings` renders as a read failure with no destructive remedy.

chunk_findings.detail: The new TOML branch drops the previous `errors="replace"` and reads with `path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` inside a `try` that only catches `(OSError, tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)`. `UnicodeDecodeError` is not a subclass of `OSError` nor of `TOMLDecodeError` (it derives from `UnicodeError` → `ValueError`), so an existing MCP file whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 makes `mcp_registered` raise instead of returning `None`. Concretely, for the codex harness (`h.mcp.shape == SHAPE_TOML`), a `config.toml` written as UTF-16 (or containing any stray high byte, e.g. `0xFF`) makes `ddflow harness doctor` / any caller of `harness_view` abort with a traceback rather than emitting the intended `"<path> cannot be read"` finding with empty remedy. The docstring explicitly promises "None when the file exists and cannot be read", and the sibling test only covers the JSON branch (`h.mcp.shape != SHAPE_TOML`), so this path is untested. Catching `UnicodeDecodeError` (or `ValueError`, or restoring `errors="replace"`) is needed.

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-change resolution chain in `sessions.py` was `("DDFLOW_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID")`. After this change the chain is built from `HR.session_env_vars()`, which is seeded with `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV[0]` (`DDFLOW_SESSION_ID`), then the descriptors' `[env] session_id` entries, then `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` — and `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` is `("DDFLOW_SESSION_ID", "CLAUDE_SESSION_ID")`. `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` has been dropped from the fallback list entirely, yet the comment directly above it claims these are "Environment variables an older ddflow or another tool already set for a session id; kept after the descriptors' so nothing that worked stops working". Concrete input: a Claude Code process that exports `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (and not `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID`), on an install where the descriptors' `[env] session_id` lists do not include it (or where `load()` yields nothing, e.g. a broken/absent descriptor directory). Before the change, line 198 turned that variable into the harness session id and the session was attributed (`return hid, "harness"`); now the loop never looks at it, the session id is not found in `live`, and the session silently falls through to the `"implicit"` branch with `HR.detect` also unable to name the harness. Either the descriptor for Claude is assumed to re-declare the variable — in which case the CLAUDE_SESSION_ID retained in `LEGACY_SESSION_ENV` is dead weight and the asymmetry is unexplained — or this is a compat regression that contradicts the stated intent of the very constant that was added.

chunk_findings.detail: The change states that "today only CLAUDE_SESSION_ID / CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID are read", and `test_every_descriptor_variable_is_consulted_in_resolution_order` confirms both Claude variables are known session variables (`"CLAUDE_SESSION_ID" in vars_` plus the "every descriptor variable is consulted" loop). Yet no test asserts what `detect()` returns for a Claude variable at all — the only detection cases exercised are GEMINI and QWEN_CODE — and the only ambiguity case is two variables belonging to *different* harnesses. A Claude Code process that exports both `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (i.e. two known variables, one harness) hits the exact shape that `detect()` is asserted to answer with `""` for two variables at once. chunk_findings.detail: For every `harness_*` action the payload is the single tuple `("harnesses", "id", "levels", "features", "findings")`, but the three subcommands that the same conditional dispatches to produce disjoint fact sets: `harness_list` returns the `harnesses` list, `harness_show` returns `id`/`levels`/`features`, and `harness_doctor` returns `findings`. The `payload` is documented as "the FACTS" from which the JSON body is built (and `message` is deliberately absent from it so it "stays OUT of the JSON body"), i.e. the body builder resolves each declared key against `data`. Given `ddflow_hooks(action="harness_list")` the body builder is therefore handed `id`, `levels`, `features` and `findings`, none of which the list result carries (the same for `harness_doctor` with `id`/`levels`/`features`/`harnesses`), so the call raises `KeyError` — or, if the builder happens to tolerate absent keys, it emits null fact fields that were never computed, contradicting the intended per-subcommand output ("list: agents and whether adopted here; show <id>: … levels … and features; doctor: drift, dangling commands, missing hooks"). The sibling CLI handler `cmd_harness` (ddflow/surfaces/commands/harness.py:14) avoids exactly this by passing only `tuple(k for k in out.data if k != "message")`; the declared payload needs the same per-action scoping instead of one union tuple.

chunk_findings.detail: The dispatcher routes to this helper whenever *any* of `--claude`, `--gemini` or `--harness <id>` is set, so a combined invocation is accepted, but the helper only forwards `harness` to the style-writer path when *both* `claude` and `gemini` are false; otherwise `harness` is dropped on the floor and `_agent_hooks(repo, action, claude=claude, gemini=gemini)` runs instead. Input: `ddflow hooks install --claude --harness copilot`. Result: the Claude entry is written, `_harness_hooks`/`HW.apply` is never called for copilot, no `--harness` writer runs, and the returned outcome is `O.ok(...)` with no mention of the skipped harness — the user is told the operation succeeded while one of the explicitly requested configurations was silently not applied. A user asking for two styles in one command (exactly what "writers by style, not by agent" invites) gets a success exit code and half the job.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring states "a style with no writer is refused", and the parallel "this ddflow cannot do what you asked, nothing is broken" case in `_agent_hooks_outcome` (`CH.NewerSettings`) is deliberately mapped to `O.refused("hooks", ..., message=..., installed=...)` with the comment "upgrade, not a failure". This branch instead returns `O.failed("hooks", why, message=why, installed=E.installed(repo))`. Input: `ddflow hooks install --harness <id whose descriptor style has no writer>`. The command installs nothing but reports a *failure* rather than a refusal, so scripts/automation that distinguish the two (and that keep going on a refusal, cf. the NewerSettings path) treat an unimplemented-but-harmless style as a hard error, contradicting the contract the function itself documents.

The writer is documented (and the change's intent states) as chosen by the descriptor's `style`/`file`/`events`, "not by agent name", and `unsupported()` exists precisely to refuse a harness whose descriptor cannot be written. But `specs()` short-circuits on the built-in table before ever consulting the descriptor:

    if table := tuple(s for s in CH.HOOKS if s.agent == h.id):
        return table

Any harness whose id is `claude` (or `gemini`) therefore keeps writing the table's file/events even when its descriptor says otherwise. Concretely, a descriptor with `[hooks] style = "none"` (the operator disabling hooks for that harness), `hooks` absent/None, or `file = ".claude/settings.local.json"` will still cause `apply()` to install the table rows into `.claude/settings.json`: `specs()` returns the table, `rows` is non-empty, and `apply()`'s `raise Unsupported(...)` is never reached, so the `"none" has nothing to install` / "not VERIFIED" / file checks are bypassed. Either the descriptor is authoritative (then the table branch must be gated by `unsupported(h)` and must not override `hk.file`/`hk.events`), or the module cannot claim descriptor-driven selection.

chunk_findings.detail:
The guard that is supposed to reject non-project files only rejects a bare `~` prefix and non-`.json` names:

    if not hk.file.endswith(".json") or hk.file.startswith("~"):
        return f"{h.id}: its hook file {hk.file} is not a project JSON file ddflow writes"

The message claims project-only enforcement, but an expanded user-scope path such as `[REDACTED:path]`, a Windows path `C:\Users\u\...\hooks.json`, `${HOME}/...`, or any `../`-escaping relative path ends with `.json` and does not start with `~`, so `unsupported()` returns `""` and `apply()` installs/uninstalls in that location (this matters directly for the VS Code/harness user-scope path called out in the session context). The same spelling inconsistency means `[REDACTED:path]` is refused while the equivalent absolute path is accepted, so install and status disagree about whether the harness is supported.

chunk_findings.detail: `fix_for` is keyed by settings-file path and built with a dict comprehension, so it is last-wins: when more than one hook spec in `rows` has the same `s.file`, only the flag of the last spec survives. `check_settings` then emits that single command as the remedy for *any* dangling ddflow command found in that file. The generalisation in this change makes shared files realistic: the session-context states that the Local/VS Code harness reads `.claude/settings.json` hooks and that VS Code's hooks live under `.github/hooks/*.json`, so a descriptor for that harness can declare the same file (or `.github/hooks` dir) as the claude-json (or copilot) descriptor. Concretely, if `rows` contains `spec(file=".claude/settings.json", flag="--claude")` followed by `spec(file=".claude/settings.json", flag="--harness vscode")`, a dangling command that came from the claude-json install is reported with the fix `ddflow hooks install --harness vscode`; running it reinstalls the wrong style and leaves the flagged command in place (the reverse ordering silently prefers `--claude` for the vscode-owned entry). The pre-change code could not hit this because the fix was computed per-path from a single `HOOKS` table with an explicit `gemini` branch. Keying the fix by marker (or collecting all flags for a shared file) would preserve the correct remedy.

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that installing the "cursor" harness is refused with `no hook writer for harness 'cursor'` (exit 1, no `.cursor` created), but the stated intent of this change lists "cursor hooks" as one of the writer styles that the descriptor chooses between: "Hook config writers by style, not by agent: claude-json, copilot hooks dir, codex hooks.json, cursor hooks, opencode plugin, none." If the cursor-harness descriptor's style is the "cursor hooks" style (the only reading under which that listed style is used by any harness), then `ddflow hooks install --harness cursor` in a repo exits 0 and writes the cursor hook file, so `assert code == 1` fails. If instead the implementation really has no cursor writer, then the cursor style listed in the intent is not implemented at all. Either way the change is internally inconsistent: the test can only pass if the "cursor hooks" style promised by the intent does not exist, and it fails as soon as that writer is present. Concretely: a repo where `HR.get("cursor").hooks.style == "cursor"` makes line 66's command succeed, breaking line 67's `assert code == 1` and the "no hook writer" message check on line 68.

chunk_findings.detail: The reordered `specs()` makes the descriptor authoritative only in the *unsupported* case: `if unsupported(h): return ()` is checked before the table, but a descriptor that IS supported and simply differs from the table still falls through to `if table := tuple(s for s in CH.HOOKS if s.agent == h.id): return table`. The comment claims "the descriptor is authoritative, the table included", yet for any harness whose id collides with a table agent (`claude`, `gemini`) the table's `CH.HookSpec` rows (their file and events) are returned and the descriptor's `style`/`file`/`events` are ignored. The newly added dispatch makes this reachable in a damaging way: `apply()` and `state()` now compute `style = h.hooks.style` and, when that style is in `FLAT_LIST`, call `flatlist.install`/`flatlist.state`/`flatlist.uninstall` with the *table* specs. Concretely, a harness whose descriptor gives `id="claude"`, a flat-list style (e.g. the Copilot/VS Code layout the session-context describes) and file `.github/hooks/x.json` passes `unsupported()` (style is in `FLAT_LIST`, file is project-relative), so `specs()` returns the Claude table rows and `apply("install")` writes them through `flatlist.install` — the flat-list writer is handed Claude specs (wrong events, and `s.file`/`s.agent` from the table) instead of the descriptor's generated rows, i.e. the wrong file/layout is written, exactly the failure mode the reorder's comment says it prevents. The probe cited for earlier finding 3 (`test_the_descriptor_outranks_the_table`) only exercises an *unsupported* descriptor (otherwise the table would still win and the test would not pass), so it does not answer this case; the fix should select the table only when the descriptor's style matches the table's style (or drop the table for the authoritatively-described case) rather than only short-circuiting on `unsupported()`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_entries` deliberately treats a `hooks` value of `null` as "no hooks" (`if hooks is None: return []`, line 28), so an existing file such as `.cursor/hooks.json` containing `{"version": 1, "hooks": null}` (valid JSON, `_read` returns the parsed dict) skips `install`'s update loop entirely and reaches line 62. There `data.setdefault("version", 1)` is a no-op and line 63 does `data.setdefault("hooks", {})` — but `dict.setdefault` does **not** replace a key that already exists with value `None`, so `hooks` stays `None` and line 64 (`hooks.setdefault(h.event, []).append(...)`) raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'setdefault'`, i.e. an unhandled traceback instead of either the graceful refusal this module promises ("a file that does not parse is never rewritten") or a repair. The inconsistency is inside the module: on the *same* input `uninstall` returns "no ddflow `<event>` hook in ..." and `state` returns `(False, "")`, because both only go through `_entries` and never touch line 63, so the three entry points disagree about what `"hooks": null` means. Fix by treating `None` as missing in the append path too (e.g. `if not isinstance(data.get("hooks"), dict): data["hooks"] = {}`), or by refusing `None` in `_entries` with a `CH.SettingsError` like the non-list case on line 30 already does.

chunk_findings.detail: The new function documents its contract as "a style with no writer is refused" (and the change intent repeats "a style with no writer is refused"), but the `HW.Unsupported` branch returns `O.failed("hooks", why, message=why, installed=E.installed(repo))`, while the very next branches in the same helper return `O.refused(...)` for `CH.NewerSettings`. chunk_findings.detail: `unsupported()` is the only barrier between a descriptor's `[hooks].file` and a write, and it only rejects two shapes: a missing `.json` suffix and a literal leading `~`. Its own error message claims the rule is "not a **project** JSON file ddflow writes", but the test does not enforce containment in the repo at all. Concretely: a descriptor with `style = "claude"`, `file = "[REDACTED:path]"` (or `"../outside.json"`, or a Windows `C:\...json`) passes `not hk.file.endswith(".json") or hk.file.startswith("~")` as false, so `unsupported()` returns `""`, `specs()` generates rows, and `apply()` calls `CH.install_spec(repo, s)`. `pathlib`'s join discards `repo` for an absolute operand, so the hook is written to the user's real global config during a repo-scoped `install` (and silently removed by `uninstall`), i.e. the class of user-scope write the guard was added to prevent. This is not hypothetical for the case the session-context singles out: VS Code user scope is an absolute path, which on many platforms does not begin with `~`, so the explicit `~` check catches only one spelling of the very thing it is meant to refuse. The check should reject any path that is not repo-relative (e.g. via `Path(hk.file).is_absolute()` plus `PurePosixPath(hk.file).parts[0] != ".."`), not just the tilde spelling.

chunk_findings.detail: The new argument `harness=harness if harness not in ("claude", "gemini") else ""` drops the requested harness name for both `claude` *and* `gemini`, but only `claude` is compensated for: the very next line sets `claude=True` when `harness == "claude"`, whereas nothing anywhere in this call carries the gemini request. `harness` came from `getattr(a, "harness", "")`, and the only other selector passed to `A.hooks` is the `claude` boolean. So for the input `ddflow hooks install --harness gemini` the call becomes `A.hooks(..., harness="", claude=False, ...)`, i.e. indistinguishable from a bare `ddflow hooks install` with no harness at all. Now that writers are selected by descriptor/style (the point of this change), the gemini writer is never selected by name; the request silently falls through to the default writer (or to nothing), and because the previous `if harness and harness not in ("claude", "gemini"): ... return FAIL` guard was removed, the user gets no error indicating gemini was ignored. The `("claude", "gemini")` tuple looks copied verbatim from the guard that was deleted; the pass-through should exclude only `claude` (or gemini needs its own flag/argument).

chunk_findings.detail:
The change's own intent states the writers are selected "by style" and enumerates the styles it implements as "claude-json, copilot hooks dir, codex hooks.json, **cursor hooks**, opencode plugin, none" — i.e. `cursor` is one of the styles this change is supposed to ship a writer for. This test instead hard-codes `cursor` as the canonical example of a harness that has *no* writer:

```python
code, out, err = run_cli(repo, "hooks", "install", "--harness", "cursor")
assert code == 1
assert "no hook writer for harness 'cursor'" in out + err and not (repo / ".cursor").exists()
```

Given the stated intent, either the implementation registers a `cursor hooks` writer (in which case this test fails: `code` will be `0`, output will not contain "no hook writer", and `.cursor/…` will be created) or it does not (in which case the change does not deliver the "cursor hooks" style it claims). One of the two is necessarily wrong; the test encodes the opposite of the delivered feature, so it is either a guaranteed red test or evidence the cursor writer is missing. No input other than simply running the suite is needed to expose this.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite turns the old "no selector means every descriptor-named harness" path into a silent no-op. The surface passes `harness` as `getattr(a, "harness", "")` (unchanged by this diff; that is the premise the previous gemini finding was triaged against), and for a plain `ddflow hooks install` / `ddflow hooks uninstall` that yields `claude=False, gemini=False, harness=""`. In the old body the `not (claude or gemini)` branch forwarded that call to `_harness_hooks(repo, action, harness)` verbatim, and the old docstring's "the Claude/Gemini flags, or any harness the descriptors name" describes exactly that empty-selector case (install for every harness the descriptors name). In the new body the `if harness:` test is a truthiness test, so `""` takes the "nothing requested" branch: `_harness_hooks` is never called, `msgs` stays empty, and the function returns `O.ok("hooks", message="", installed=E.installed(repo))` — exit 0, empty message, no hooks written. The caller cannot distinguish this from "everything already up to date". The guard needs to distinguish "selector omitted" (`harness == ""`) from "this selector value is irrelevant because claude/gemini was already handled", e.g. by calling `_harness_hooks` whenever `not (claude or gemini)` as before, or by having the surface pass an explicit sentinel for the no-selector case.

chunk_findings.detail: `_entries` explicitly treats a top-level `"hooks": null` as "no hooks yet" (line 27-29: `hooks = data.get("hooks")`, `if hooks is None: return []`), so `install` proceeds to the add branch for such a file. But `dict.setdefault` only fills in a key that is *absent*; when the key is present with value `None`, `data.setdefault("hooks", {})` returns `None`, and the very next line `hooks.setdefault(h.event, []).append(...)` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'setdefault'`. Input that demonstrates it: a descriptor with `style = "cursor"` (or `copilot`), `file = ".cursor/hooks.json"`, and the existing file containing `{"version": 1, "hooks": null}`; `ddflow hooks install` reaches line 64 and dies with an unhandled traceback instead of either refusing the file or creating the list. This also contradicts the file's own contract that a non-conforming structure is refused and the intent's "refuse unparsable files as today" behaviour (`uninstall` on the same file returns "no ddflow hook" cleanly, so the two writers disagree about what `hooks: null` means). A guard such as `hooks = data.get("hooks"); if not isinstance(hooks, dict): hooks = data["hooks"] = {}` (or raising `CH.SettingsError`) is needed before the append.

chunk_findings.detail: The dispatcher routes to this helper whenever *any* of `--claude`, `--gemini` or `--harness <id>` is set, so a combined invocation is accepted, but the helper only forwards `harness` to the style-writer path when *both* `claude` and `gemini` are false; otherwise `harness` is dropped on the floor and `_agent_hooks(repo, action, claude=claude, gemini=gemini)` runs instead. Input: `ddflow hooks install --claude --harness copilot`. A user asking for two styles in one command (exactly what "writers by style, not by agent" invites) gets a success exit code and half the job.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring states "a style with no writer is refused", and the parallel "this ddflow cannot do what you asked, nothing is broken" case in `_agent_hooks_outcome` (`CH.NewerSettings`) is deliberately mapped to `O.refused("hooks", ..., message=..., installed=...)` with the comment "upgrade, not a failure". Concretely: a descriptor with `style = "claude"`, `file = "[REDACTED:path]"` (or `"../outside.json"`, or a Windows `C:\...json`) passes `not hk.file.endswith(".json") or hk.file.startswith("~")` as false, so `unsupported()` returns `""`, `specs()` generates rows, and `apply()` calls `CH.install_spec(repo, s)`. `pathlib`'s join discards `repo` for an absolute operand, so the hook is written to the user's real global config during a repo-scoped `install` (and silently removed by `uninstall`), i.e. the class of user-scope write the guard was added to prevent. This is not hypothetical for the case the session-context singles out: VS Code user scope is an absolute path, which on many platforms does not begin with `~`, so the explicit `~` check catches only one spelling of the very thing it is meant to refuse. The check should reject any path that is not repo-relative (e.g. via `Path(hk.file).is_absolute()` plus `PurePosixPath(hk.file).parts[0] != ".."`), not just the tilde spelling.

chunk_findings.detail: The new argument `harness=harness if harness not in ("claude", "gemini") else ""` drops the requested harness name for both `claude` *and* `gemini`, but only `claude` is compensated for: the very next line sets `claude=True` when `harness == "claude"`, whereas nothing anywhere in this call carries the gemini request. `harness` came from `getattr(a, "harness", "")`, and the only other selector passed to `A.hooks` is the `claude` boolean. So for the input `ddflow hooks install --harness gemini` the call becomes `A.hooks(..., harness="", claude=False, ...)`, i.e. indistinguishable from a bare `ddflow hooks install` with no harness at all. Now that writers are selected by descriptor/style (the point of this change), the gemini writer is never selected by name; the request silently falls through to the default writer (or to nothing), and because the previous `if harness and harness not in ("claude", "gemini"): ... return FAIL` guard was removed, the user gets no error indicating gemini was ignored. The `("claude", "gemini")` tuple looks copied verbatim from the guard that was deleted; the pass-through should exclude only `claude` (or gemini needs its own flag/argument).

chunk_findings.detail:
The change's own intent states the writers are selected "by style" and enumerates the styles it implements as "claude-json, copilot hooks dir, codex hooks.json, **cursor hooks**, opencode plugin, none" — i.e. `cursor` is one of the styles this change is supposed to ship a writer for. This test instead hard-codes `cursor` as the canonical example of a harness that has *no* writer:

```python
code, out, err = run_cli(repo, "hooks", "install", "--harness", "cursor")
assert code == 1
assert "no hook writer for harness 'cursor'" in out + err and not (repo / ".cursor").exists()
```

Given the stated intent, either the implementation registers a `cursor hooks` writer (in which case this test fails: `code` will be `0`, output will not contain "no hook writer", and `.cursor/…` will be created) or it does not (in which case the change does not deliver the "cursor hooks" style it claims). One of the two is necessarily wrong; the test encodes the opposite of the delivered feature, so it is either a guaranteed red test or evidence the cursor writer is missing. No input other than simply running the suite is needed to expose this.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite turns the old "no selector means every descriptor-named harness" path into a silent no-op. The surface passes `harness` as `getattr(a, "harness", "")` (unchanged by this diff; that is the premise the previous gemini finding was triaged against), and for a plain `ddflow hooks install` / `ddflow hooks uninstall` that yields `claude=False, gemini=False, harness=""`. In the old body the `not (claude or gemini)` branch forwarded that call to `_harness_hooks(repo, action, harness)` verbatim, and the old docstring's "the Claude/Gemini flags, or any harness the descriptors name" describes exactly that empty-selector case (install for every harness the descriptors name). In the new body the `if harness:` test is a truthiness test, so `""` takes the "nothing requested" branch: `_harness_hooks` is never called, `msgs` stays empty, and the function returns `O.ok("hooks", message="", installed=E.installed(repo))` — exit 0, empty message, no hooks written. The caller cannot distinguish this from "everything already up to date". The guard needs to distinguish "selector omitted" (`harness == ""`) from "this selector value is irrelevant because claude/gemini was already handled", e.g. by calling `_harness_hooks` whenever `not (claude or gemini)` as before, or by having the surface pass an explicit sentinel for the no-selector case.

chunk_findings.detail: `_entries` explicitly treats a top-level `"hooks": null` as "no hooks yet" (line 27-29: `hooks = data.get("hooks")`, `if hooks is None: return []`), so `install` proceeds to the add branch for such a file. But `dict.setdefault` only fills in a key that is *absent*; when the key is present with value `None`, `data.setdefault("hooks", {})` returns `None`, and the very next line `hooks.setdefault(h.event, []).append(...)` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'setdefault'`. Input that demonstrates it: a descriptor with `style = "cursor"` (or `copilot`), `file = ".cursor/hooks.json"`, and the existing file containing `{"version": 1, "hooks": null}`; `ddflow hooks install` reaches line 64 and dies with an unhandled traceback instead of either refusing the file or creating the list. This also contradicts the file's own contract that a non-conforming structure is refused and the intent's "refuse unparsable files as today" behaviour (`uninstall` on the same file returns "no ddflow hook" cleanly, so the two writers disagree about what `hooks: null` means). A guard such as `hooks = data.get("hooks"); if not isinstance(hooks, dict): hooks = data["hooks"] = {}` (or raising `CH.SettingsError`) is needed before the append.
